_comment: Prices verified 2026-10-13. Every url is the official pricing page so a
rise is one click away rather than a rumour. Re-check before paying.
CKS cannot be attempted before CKA has been passed.

items.title: 1. AWS Solutions Architect – Associate — $150
items.note: 130 min, 65 questions, valid 3 years. Take it first: cheapest by a factor of three, and OffSec discount Learn One up to 20% for existing holders.

items.title: 2. CKA — $445, or $645 with the LFS258 course
items.note: Valid 2 years. One retake and two Killer.sh attempts included, 12 months to schedule. Skip the course upgrade if you already operate clusters. Gates CKS.

items.title: 3. CKS — $445, or $645 with the LFS260 course
items.note: Requires a passed CKA first — the only hard ordering constraint. Valid 2 years. The course upgrade is worth it here in a way it is not for CKA.

items.title: 4. OSCP — $1,749 bundle, or $2,749/yr Learn One
items.note: Lifetime. The bundle is 90 days of lab access and ONE exam attempt; Learn One gives two attempts and a year, which beats failing and rebuying.

_comment: The standing tasks below run every day. The variant on top rotates the
bounty-agent work, so the tool gets built by using it rather than in a
separate project that never ships.
Hand-solve appears twice on purpose. The rotation weights, it does not
sequence — and the build guide is explicit that you solve challenges by
hand BEFORE automating, because otherwise you cannot tell whether the
agent is missing bugs or your prompts are bad. Drop the second entry once
you have five hand-written PoCs.
Order matters only for where the cycle starts: the variant index is
ordinal % len, so this list was rotated on 2026-09-17 to open on
Hand-solve. Benchmark needs a hand-solved target to compare against, and
Gate needs a report.json to read. Reorder freely once both exist.
remind=false means tracked and shown on /day, never a reminder. Stated
priority is RareSkills and the fellowship; the rest is there when there is
room, which is the difference between a backlog and a nag.

_comment: Morning reading, 05:00. Political rather than technical on purpose:
the three priorities already own the deep blocks, and the half hour
that opens the day is the one reliably quiet slot there is.
A starting list, not a prescription — swap any of it. One book stays
filed until you advance the cursor, which at thirty minutes a day is
roughly a fortnight each.
tracks.label: Morning reading

items.title: The Dictator's Handbook — Bueno de Mesquita & Smith
items.note: Power as a coalition problem. The clearest model of why institutions behave as they do, and it transfers directly to how organisations work.

items.title: Why Nations Fail — Acemoglu & Robinson
items.note: Extractive versus inclusive institutions. The book most often cited badly — read it so you can tell.

items.title: Seeing Like a State — James C. Scott
items.note: Why top-down schemes to improve things fail. The most useful book on this list for an engineer.

items.title: The Prince — Machiavelli
items.note: Short, free, and almost nothing like its reputation. Read the text rather than the quotes.

items.title: The Origins of Political Order — Fukuyama
items.note: How states, rule of law and accountability actually arose. Long; a fortnight at this pace is optimistic.

items.title: The Narrow Corridor — Acemoglu & Robinson
items.note: The sequel argument: liberty as a balance between state and society rather than an end state.

items.title: How Democracies Die — Levitsky & Ziblatt
items.note: The slow, procedural version of collapse rather than the dramatic one.

items.title: On Tyranny — Timothy Snyder
items.note: Twenty short lessons. Two or three mornings total — a good palate cleanser between the long ones.

items.title: The Open Society and Its Enemies — Popper
items.note: The case against historical inevitability, and the best argument for falsifiability outside science.

items.title: The Power Broker — Robert Caro
items.note: One man, unelected, reshaping a city. The finest case study of informal power ever written. Very long.

items.title: Political Order and Political Decay — Fukuyama
items.note: The modern half: how functioning institutions rot.

items.title: Rules for Radicals — Saul Alinsky
items.note: Organising from the outside. Read alongside the Dictator's Handbook — same mechanics, opposite vantage point.

_comment: Four weeks to SAA-C03, in the order the exam rewards.
Booking comes before studying on purpose: the booking is what makes it
a deadline, and without one this slips. The voucher check is first
because ten minutes there can halve the $150.
VPC sits early because it is the hardest domain and the one most
failures come from — it belongs in a fresh brain, not week three.
The last three items are practice exams, not reading. SAA is a
question-reading exam as much as a knowledge exam, and the review item
between the two is where the marks actually come from.
tracks.label: AWS SAA

items.title: Check for a voucher before you pay
items.note: Ten minutes. AWS Certification account -> benefits for a 50% voucher, and check Pearson VUE for a running promotion. Could halve the $150.

items.title: Book the exam, online-proctored, four weeks out
items.note: $150, 130 min, 65 questions. OnVUE from home needs a quiet room, clear desk, photo ID. The booking is the deadline — everything after this is against a clock.

items.title: Read the exam guide end to end
items.note: The actual syllabus. Secure 30%, resilient 26%, high-performing 24%, cost-optimised 20% — study in proportion to that, not to interest.

items.title: Start the official Skill Builder prep plan
items.note: AWS's own four-step plan. Run it alongside the items below rather than instead of them.

items.title: IAM: users, roles, policies
items.note: Roles vs users is the single most tested distinction. Know trust policy vs permission policy cold.

items.title: VPC: subnets, routing, NAT, SG vs NACL
items.note: The hardest domain and where most failures come from. Draw one by hand: public/private subnets, IGW, NAT, route tables. Stateful SG vs stateless NACL.

items.title: EC2: families, purchasing options, placement
items.note: On-demand vs reserved vs spot vs savings plans is a cost-domain question in disguise.

items.title: S3: storage classes, lifecycle, encryption
items.note: Storage classes and lifecycle rules appear in both the cost and resilience domains. Know retrieval times for Glacier tiers.

items.title: EBS vs EFS vs instance store
items.note: A question type, not a topic: 'shared across instances' means EFS, 'ephemeral' means instance store.

items.title: RDS and Aurora: multi-AZ vs read replicas
items.note: Multi-AZ is availability, read replicas are scale. Exams punish confusing the two.

items.title: DynamoDB: keys, indexes, capacity
items.note: Partition key design, GSI vs LSI, on-demand vs provisioned, and when DAX is the answer.

items.title: Load balancers and Auto Scaling
items.note: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB by layer and use case. Scaling policies: target tracking, step, scheduled.

items.title: SQS, SNS and EventBridge: decoupling
items.note: You have built this on Workers and queues already — map it across. Standard vs FIFO, DLQs, fan-out.

items.title: Lambda and API Gateway
items.note: Limits and concurrency are the examinable part. The closest thing to what you already run on Workers.

items.title: Resilience and DR: RTO, RPO, the four strategies
items.note: Backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site. Scenario questions give you an RTO and expect the cheapest strategy that meets it.

items.title: KMS, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store
items.note: Encryption at rest and in transit, key rotation, and when Secrets Manager beats Parameter Store (rotation, and it costs more).

items.title: CloudFront and Route 53
items.note: Routing policies — simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation — are near-guaranteed marks. Learn OAC for private S3 origins.

items.title: Cost: the 20% everyone leaves until last
items.note: Savings Plans vs RIs, S3 class transitions, and data transfer — egress is the charge that surprises people. Price one of your own designs.

items.title: The Well-Architected Framework
items.note: The vocabulary the exam and interviewers both use. Run a real review against something you own — an audit with findings, not reading.

items.title: First full timed practice exam
items.note: Full 130 minutes, no pausing. The score matters less than which domain is weakest — that is what week four is for.

items.title: Review every wrong answer
items.note: Write why each distractor is wrong, not just why the right one is right. This item is where the marks come from.

items.title: Second practice exam, fresh questions
items.note: Gate: 85%+ consistently before you sit it. Below that you are gambling $150 to save a week.

_comment: An ordered curriculum, not a rotation. The cursor moves when an item is
finished, not when the date changes — that is the whole difference.
The cursor lives in the database, not here, because progress is state and
a container restart would lose it. This file holds the order; the order
is the opinion and belongs in git.
